This type of statement is exactly what I would expect to see from
frequent visitors to this group.

So as everyone chimes in that a cash prize would ruin VTES, I would
say that I support it.

I used to play in all the big events. The reasons were the challenge
(primary) and then prizes (a far, far second). Well, WW has always
really sucked big time when it came to providing prizes for VTES.
Once I made it to the NAC final table, this was the end of the
challenge for me. When I saw LSJ give out a box of boosters and some
lame ass promo stuff to the Top 5 players, end of the line for me. It
was simple math at that point. I paid $250+/ea or so dollars to go to
a Qualifier Tournament (or two). Then I paid $1500 to go to Gencon.
I walk away with 18 booster packs. At that point, without the
challenge aspect, all I had was a quest for prizes. It quickly dawned
on me that I could save time and money by just staying home. I could
then spend the $1750 on $65 booster boxes of cards and get around 30
boxes (1080 booster packs).

So I've been staying home. However, the booster pack logic has taken
a new twist. Since I no longer have to stay uber competitive, I no
longer buy any cards. I used to drop hundreds of dollars on each new
release by WW. It's now been 3-4 sets that I have just gone to a
prerelease and not placed my order. That's probably $1000 of my money
that WW has lost-and will continue to not capture. Plus since I no
longer have to playtest high level tournament decks, I no longer make
the effort to assemble a local playgroup. I used to run one that had
8-12 players, weekly playnights, monthly tournaments. How many of
those players did I influence to buy cards? We would pool orders to
get discounts and save on shipping. So how much money was I making
for WW both directly and indirectly? Hard to tell really. It's much
easier on my wallet these days because I can take my huge pile of
cards and make a good deck that can win local tournaments.

Therefore, if WW was to offer larger cash prizes for the bigger
events, I would be tempted to get back up to speed and attend these
events. It doesn't have to be $25,000 dollars. But as long as the
"break even" ratio still points to staying home, I'm home. So if you
want to keep this game rolling along the SAME as it's always been,
feel free to continue to offer lame ass prizes. Sure, it's obvious
that there are 50-75 people who will keep attending these events year
after year (has anyone seen the attendance at Regional/higher level
events increase in a significant manner over the last seven
years???). It's obvious that WW lets personal opinions of certain
people make business decisions. It's obvious this game is stale
regarding the upper level tournament structure. But please, continue
to be horrified at the simple notion of offering more than half a box
of boosters to the winner of the NAC. Maybe LA's ideas are the start
of something. Still not enough to get me, or any of the local players
I know, to spend the time/money and attend larger events. Plus the
final kicker of it all is that the couple of people I know who do play
VTES and might attend the larger events, will be playing other games
instead that do have larger prizes (there is only so much time at a
convention-so you could play 18hrs of VTES over two days or multiple
VS/Magic events-win the VTES and get a promo card, with the VS/Magic
event and pay for a year of college). Look around, people are so
saturated with CCG's that offering money payouts are now the standard
(which brings us back full circle to EVE). If you don't do that, it's
like bringing a new 2008 model car to market without A/C. Who's going
to buy that? Maybe I'm in the minority (at least here I am as most of
the players I know don't even bother to read this group).

It's nice to see that fear of change still rules and kills a
discussion before it's even started.

Ben.S.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <1185369488....@l70g2000hse.googlegroups.com>,
bspaul <bspa...@excite.com> wrote:

There is a difference between a "cash prize" and a "big cash prize". I
in no way think that it would be bad to have prizes in the $100.00 zone
for big tournaments (like, a couple box of boosters, or some cash or
something). But really, due to the structure of the game, a significant
cash prize *really* would make the game into something significantly
different than it is now, and not necessarily in a good way.

VTES is a free form, multi player game. Where folks can do arbitrary
things to totally hose other players that are usually dis-incentived by
virtue of it not being in their own best interest. When you, in the
finals, can say "Hey--guy with the Rush deck, if you cross table destroy
my predator and I win, I'll hand you $1000.00...", the game does not
become about the stated goals of the game--i.e. ousting your prey,
getting as many VPs as you can, and trying to get a game win.

The game *already* teeters dangerously close to being too arbitrary and
kingmakery, where the guy who wins the tournament is not the guy who can
build the best deck and can play the game the best, but is the guy who
is best at convincing their opponents to do things that are not in their
best interest. If you added in "and I'll give you a significant sum of
money if you help me win", the game ceases to be the game it is designed
to be.

Two player, duel type games are very well suited for significant cash
prizes, as diplomacy is not an issue. Multiplayer games, where diplomacy
and table talk and dealmaking are an accepted part of the game and can
determine who wins more often than not (see, in poker, you don't
generally see someone saying "Hey--I see how you are beating me with
that flush, but if you fold this hand so I can take the pot, I'll split
the winnings with you when I win the table...") are not very well suited
for significant cash prize environments. As the game ceases to be about
the actual game, and becomes "who can buy their way to victory with
promises of a cut of the winnings." Which isn't VTES.

Nice post. I agree with most of it. When I used to play Magic, toward
the end, I was just in it for the money. It definitely wasn't the
fame, because who really cares to be known by Magic trolls? And by
the time I stopped playing Magic, I hadn't been playing for the love

nuts when they're mismanaged. Frankly, given the fates of Magi
Nation, DBZ, and Battlestar Galactica (all of which were as good if
not better than VTES, mechanically, despite some of their...content),
I'm sometimes surprised VTES has lasted this long, frankly. Don't get
me wrong: VTES is a great game. But if the aforementioned games teach
us one thing, it's that good games don't necessarily survive
startlingly poor management.

White Wolf has never done anything special to support VTES. Releasing
sets every now and then doesn't even register. Cash prizes,
tournament organization, real promotional materials (that are
attractive to both existing and potential players), and sponsoring
nifty events are a good start.

small yet loyal base of VTES players, which would be fine in a cozy-
kind-of-way except for the fact that the players have not changed
significantly in years. So, because there's no new blood drawn into
the game with cash prizes, events, etc., a small, entrenched group of
players have just scooped up the game and run off with it. The want--
need--for cash prizes goes beyond anyone's personal greed or
motivations in tournaments; we, as a community who likes to play this
game, need new players. Cash prizes are how we get those players.
Period.

game" for whatever reason, it smacks of insularity and xenophobia. No
one is trying to change the rules or do anything else that would
actually change or ruin the game. The issue here is not the existence
of cash prizes, because those by themselves cannot and will not cause
problems. The real problem is the selfish, entrenched, (frankly)
boring people in charge. This is not to say that all veteran players
are mean, nasty old coots; I've met a lot of cool folks from the
Boston, NYC, and D.C. groups. But the vets who happen to have knee-
jerk negative reactions against new players and cash prizes need to
cut it out, shut up, and let the rest of us find a way to have a good
time. For some (or many), that means cash prizes. But at the very
least we will see some new faces across the table.

As cool as a tight-knit community is, it naturally breeds insularity.
New or potential players are going to be intimidated or scared-off by
that kind of coziness, at first. But cash is an incentive both within
and without the group. Oh. I can hear it now: "But that's just it!
We'll have a bunch of random people coming to qualifiers and maybe
winning!" Good! If they are that good, and they're nice folks, then
you just co-opt them into your community.

White Wolf has the money to put up for the big tourneys. They just
don't care. VTES is a player's game, and White Wolf listens to the
(few) players and gives "us" what "we" want. We just need to shake
things up so that "we" is not just a handful of entrenched xenophobes
and White Wolf knows who plays this game and what the rest of us want
out of it. I'd just like to see new players every now and then, and
anyone who tells me that they wouldn't like to win cash is a goddamn
liar.

I like this game and I'd like to continue to like it for a while. But
that means (and, again, no offense to anyone, certainly) more
players, for me. The people I play against are cool and all that, but
it would be even better to have some new folks around, right?

Chris.B.

Well, if the problem is that you are not getting enough new players
than you should try think what is going to get new players into the
game from their perspective. I can see that this is what you are
trying to do, but I don't think your rationale is quite right.

The basic problem with your argument of cash prizes = more new players
is that this market has already been well covered for by many other
card games out there who can do this sort of thing far better than
VTES can. To try put VTES into that market will certainly be forcing
VTES to play on it's hind leg, so to speak. As people have already
mentioned - duel based card games are far better at this sort of prize
structure and player mentality than VTES is.

Instead, if you want to get new players, the best way to do so is to
play to VTES strengths. VTES is a very social card game. It helps
build up a community of friendly helpful cardgamers (especially if the
people in charge foster this kind of attitude). This is what I find
refreshing about VTES and what really attracts me to the game. Over
here in Cape Town, we don't have any asshole players (anymore at
least). All of our players here want to have newbies join the game and
are always willing to help them out. Unfortunately with it's complex
rules and sheer volume of errata, VTES can be quite difficult for new
players to get a hang of, so having a more care-free attitude about
the game is more of a plus than a minus. Not to say that there isn't a
time or place for 'play-to-win' mentality, but that attitude is
generally reserved for the more experienced players when playing
amongst each other.

That being said, I think the complete opposite mentality is actually
better for attracting new players. One of VTES major strengths has
always been the fact that (comparatively) it is a very inexpensive
game to play and 99.9% of your cards will always be playable in a
tournament environment. I, for one, am running a completely free
preconstructed tournament that is focused on getting new players into
the game. There is no entrance cost, a very minor prize, but all the
players involved will be able to walk away with a preconstructed deck
that they can now play with their friends.

I'm fortunate enough to have played with all the experienced players
out here in Cape Town (and I fully realise that I am a Prince in a
city filled with really great sociable players), so I know that our
players will actually go around finding new players to join in this
event - and we already have a decently sized group of newbies who will
try out the game. I'm also incredibly grateful to Oscar who was kind
enough to send us 3rd Ed starter boxes for free in order for us to be
able to run this newbie tournament. If it wasn't for that, I'd
probably pay for some of it out of my own pocket, and raise some funds
in our tournaments to pay for the rest, but Oscar has always been very
supportive of my attempts to get new players and organise tournament
events.

My argument, as such, is that in order for you to get VTES to grow in
your community, maybe you should try thinking of playing to VTES
strengths, and realise that VTES marketed to a group of players that
(generally) wanted a game that was different from your powerhouse CCGs
like Magic. Trying to squeeze into their market is just suicidal for
the game. Instead, the strength of VTES has always been it's social
strength and it's community of fans who just want the game to grow,
and to share their love of the game with others.

In closing, if players really just wanted to play a game for great
prizes, there are far better games to do that with than VTES, and most
card players will immediately sense that by just looking at how a game
or two of VTES is played. There may be other reasons that you could
use to argue for great cash prizes, but the attraction for new players
is a rather weak point in my opinion, because there are far better
ways of attracting a better kind of new player anyway.

trying hard enough. I think it's been demonstrated over time that a box

good platform for hard-core monetary-reward-motivated competition.

have done so for EVE then they definantly need to do it for VTES. I
think the best way to discourage collusion at the finals table is
simple. Don't make it a winner take all situation. Make sure that
every finalist walks away with something. This encourages players to
try to get a higher position than anyone else on the table.

So for example if WW were to put $30,000.00 on the table as a cash
prize. The worst thing that they could do is to give all of it to the
first place player. The best way to do it would be to break it down
as follows.

1st Prize: $10,000.00
2nd Prize: $8,000.00
3rd Prize: $6,000.00
4th Prize: $4,000.00
5th Prize: $2,000.00

There is a signifigant difference between 1st place and 5th place, but
not enough difference between one prize level and the next to make
playing a 5th place "kingmaker" a better play than trying to get 4th
place instead.

Also, since I am one of the players who has actually played VTES for
money and it was not enjoyable. I will tell you specifically what
went wrong.

First, I played in 1996 for money at a 12 person tournamnet winner
take all.

These are the problems that existed then that don't exist now.
There was no errata. This game was pre 7-7 rulings.

We played on a 12 person table. Now we would have played on 3 4-
player tables.

There were no anti-collusion rules. Collusion was actually expected.
Now we have judges and rules to stop collusion from taking place.

We only played one game. Now we have 3 rounds and a final.

Now we have corrected all these problems. The only thing that seems
to rear its ugly head is the collusion rules.

How can you stop collusion? You need to give players incentives to
keep them in the game. I think that making sure that everyone at the
finals table or even top 10 walks away with something will make it
less likely that players will collude together.

I think we should try it, and if it doesn't work then we can alway
change back.

> How can you pretend that playing a "Bribery" game instead of VTES

Leveraging an otherwise legal deal with money is certainly something I
can call "bribery" tongue in cheek, but as long as all other aspects of
the game are being obeyed, there is nothing cheating about it.

Currently, there are plenty of instances where you can accept the losing
end of a deal, although without any concrete incentive, it doesn't
happen as often as it could. If there was concrete incentive (i.e.
cash), it would happen all the time.

Again, say I am in the finals and I'm not doing so hot. I have the
option of:

A) Possibly getting a VP for 4th place, or possibly just getting killed
for 5th.

or

B) Certainly getting 5th place, and helping someone else get 1st place.

Currently, with no money on the line, I have no incentive to pick (B),
so I'll always pick (A).

If the other guy I can help can offer me a split of the prize, it is
completely in my best interest to pick option (B), and I likely easily
defend my position of "I'm losing anyway, so I choose to lose like
this..." And it isn't cheating. And it can be called "bribery". Even if
only tongue in cheek.

> As far as I recall from my Magic experience, the ONLY thing that was
> allowed to do with the prize money is an agreement to split the prize
> INSTEAD of playing.

Which is all well and good, except:

A) This isn't Magic.

B) Magic is a two player game. Which is very, very different from a 5
player game.

> OK. So if I'm the richest guy here, I don't even need to play? I can
> just buy some players to play for me? REALLY???

People buy folks to play for them all the time in other games (i.e. "I'm
not the best basketball player in the world, but I want my team to win,
so I'll leverage getting this ringer on my team with money..."). But
other than that, I don't really know what you are talking about here.

> You are cheating just because you've accepted a bribery, and your
> "partner" is cheating because he suggested a bribe to you. That's
> enough to DQ both of you.

How am I cheating? If there was no money involved, I could make a deal
like that (i.e. give up a questionable position to help someone else).
How does having money in the equation suddenly make it cheating? You are
inventing rules in your head that don't currently exist.

> Who told you this? Collusion can be established during a game as well
> as any other time. Any deal that includes non-game things (money or
> something else) is a collusion.

I don't think collusion in this context means what you think it means.

> you, since Belarus is a poor country), but my reputation is much more

That is nice to say now. But given the opportunity to legally say "Huh.
I could probably lose here and get nothing or I could throw my support
behind someone else and be guaranteed money...", most folks would take
the money. And that doesn't mean they are cheating.

In tournament poker, the final two players, more often than not, agree
to a prize split rather than playing till the bitter end, as head to
head poker is a long slow process. And if someone is behind going into
that point, they have all the incentive in the world to make a
reasonable split. This is in no way cheating (unless the rules
specifically say "no final two splitting"). And if you are playing for
money, it is totally reasonable. But if you are playing for not money,
there is no incentive at all to do this--you just play to the bitter end.

> One of us must be insane.

I think we have already established that...

is a bad idea.

Time for some general comments. Some people who have responded have
confused my comments with the ones I posted from Chris.B. But this

ie PTO/Weenie-Breed Swarm, etc. and provide the evidence to get them
fixed. It might make "the old timers" elevate their play to a whole
new level. Just because someone jumps into a game just to win money
doesn't necessarily mean they are automatically going to win. Maybe
some of these new players will actually be cool folks who will also
play casual during casual games? Using money as bait doesn't imply it
will only catch "the evil assholes". People all have different
personalities, no matter if you are playing VTES for 18 booster packs
or $1800. To be honest, I've met a few assholes playing VTES. I'm
sure some people I've faced think I am a total jerk. It happens. But
I have also met some really cool people playing VTES. I don't think
that experience would change with a big cash prize, except that I
would have the opportunity to meet more people (and perhaps find more
opportunities to play games, find people to trade with, etc.).

Jeff makes a point about the reason for why Oscar was hired. In my
opinion, I don't really see any big change in the tournament scene
since he's been a WW employee. One or two more storylines, but
otherwise it's been the same as it was. Of course I am not privy to
behind the scene schemes and plans.

In summary, the general theme that has appeared in this topic is that
WW should (and can now obviously afford) do more to advertise and
promote this game. The game needs to offer more to keep it from
totally falling off the radar and doing it's impression of the slow
withering. The game has got to bring a gun to a gun fight-a knife
just doesn't do it anymore these days. VTES has to "recruit" players
just like employers have to recruit new employees. If you don't offer
the same benefits as the business across the street, you won't attract
the same number of applicants. Prizes need to be increased to not
only attract new players, but to give something back to all the "old
timer" players and keep them interested. The core group of the
hardcore players needs to open up slightly to new ideas and efforts to
bring in new players. Why not try a bigger prize pool for a year or
two and see what happens? Would such an idea really bring about
Gehenna for VTES? Let's try something new, it just might bring the
game to a whole new level. Without change, things will stay the same
(prophetic stuff isn't it?). This topic has turned into a decent
discussion. I was afraid that without some abrasiveness from me, the
topic would've been killed quite quickly by the loyal "we play for the
fun of the game because that's the way we've done it for 13 years and
it works well enough for me" crowd that tends to be the regular ones
who read this group.

That is all.

Invested... invested. how i cannot stand that word in gamer culture --
and i come across it far too often. i always reply thus: Entertainment
is not an Investment.

Gold is an investment, bonds are an investment, stocks are an
investment, property is an investment. Entertainment, being the ephemera
that it is, is not an investment... unless you are willing to sit on
your ass with it for 50+ years and then try to find a market.

my atari and nintendo games, even some of my really rare ones, are not
investments. my books, including some rare, first edition, out-of-print
gaming books, are not an investment. unless you are planning to live
your retirement as an antiquarian, all the money you pour into the
consumption -- not production -- of entertainment is an utter craps
shoot of an 'investment.' your worth should be gained soon after the
mere act of consumption; anything beyond its transient life cycle is a
bonus.

there, my pet peeve ended.

now, if you really want to talk investments, objet d'art crafted by
known artisans can be an investment. so a special order porcelain Edge
by Lladro' (costing let's say $1700) would have roughly equivalent value
inside and outside the VTES market. which, if this would suit you, would
mean that you are possibly more pleased by the idea of in-kind rewards
than untested collectible value. (it could also potentially serve as
advertisement for the game, as well.)

> I think a lot of people think that what you got for your $1700 was at
> the tournaments you attended. You paid the money and got to play good
> competive games and tournaments and some of us happen to think that's
> not too bad a deal in and of itself. For people who need a shot at
> prizes that even begin to recoup their investment in cards and travel,
> I still say this is not the game for them.

and in this i heartily agree. if you are looking for significant prize
money, or restitution of a worth equivalent to your expenses, you should
be looking at other games. you should be looking at games like
CounterStrike, MtG, Bridge, or the big granddaddy -- Poker. you need a
market so large where there's enough high money players to cater to the
compensation of elite players. vtes just doesn't have that level of
saturation. and considering the nature of the game, as explained here...

This game simply cannot be
> structured in a way that gurantees the level of fairness and impeccability
> demanded for contests involving valuable prizes. Play-to-win is just
> too nebulous, too subjective, and in some cases just plain impossible
> to judge correctly. Unfortunately, the game really relies on the
> sportsmanship of its players to avoid problems in these areas. And
> if you inject large rewards into the mix, you won't get that in some
> cases.
>
> Fred
>
>

...it's too close to a pipe dream. there's so much social fluidity and
interaction that it complicates the means to get such foundational
benchmarks.

that said, i dig the "win tix to the euro championships, in Paris! :D"
method of compensation. it's an in-kind prize that has value both inside
and outside the world of vtes. also, unlike cash prizes, you can't
divide portions of your ticketed seat to butter up in-game deals. a
mixture of both in-kind compensation prizes, and unique objects of
status, could be a good compromise in trying to ratchet up the appeal of
the game.

what i would like, though, is a community assessment on where are we
having trouble recruiting and retaining players. is it rules, game
length, etc?

players gang up on you turn one because your name is Ben for example

Fourth, bribes and collusion vs. play to win. It happens but maybe a
larger prize will help correct the problem. Think about the other
potential side of the coin. Perhaps we will see finalists going down
hill in an effort to win it all. What if the event gave the overall
winner, after the final round, $25K? Would players really start
making deals or maybe the might just play the game and try to win by
ousting their prey? It's hard to answer these questions without any
actual data to review, right?

So if a larger cash prize is necessary to get this game out of the
shadows (so to speak) and draw in new players, why not give it a try?
Start with some smaller prizes if you think big money is too drastic.
Offer plane tickets or hotel rooms or con registration fees. Why not
revise the qualifier system to offer a share of the prize pool.
Instead of supporting 12 player regional events, divide North America
into six zones each with a qualifier. The finalists at each qualifier
get a $500 or so prize, to help them get to the big event. Maybe this
would encourage players to attend the qualifiers-give them incentive
to leave their houses/local game shops/etc. and try their luck at the
larger events. Once they get a taste of the larger event environment,
maybe they might attend more of them or encourage others to attend.
Thus let's not track our thinking into the mold of larger prizes will
bring out the stereotypical "jerks" who are only playing for the
money. Let's expand into the realm of thinking that larger prizes may
bring out the people who love to play the game for the game, except
they can't afford to make the trip to the Nationals or the NAC. So in
summary, I still think that an influx of money into VTES would make a
positive difference in the game. If done wisely, along with other
well coordinated revisions to the current system, the game could move
to a new level of participation and game play. Self review and change
is not the end of the world. It's been 13 years of VTES. Are the
next 13 years going to be the same or do we try something new? What
do we have to lose?

Ben.S.

qualifier events in the U.S. - at least on the western side of the
country - is that they're the best attended tournaments and garner
as much participation as they should considering the overall level
of participation in VtES. It's the latter that's taking a beating,
lately, especially in the marginal areas. The problem with VtES is
that because you really need four players to make a decent game and
because this fact tends to make the experience - whether pick-up
play, local tournament, or qualifier - accelerate downwards the closer
you get to zero attendance, I've noticed that participation at any
given locality tends to fall off a cliff at a certain point. Groups
that play in high-volume participation areas don't really notice that
so much because no one really cares that much if they show up at a
tournament with 12 players as opposed to 15 players. It makes a lot
more difference as your tournament attendance sudden drops from eight
to five and you can't put two tables together. From there it's a
rapid decline into not being able to put together a tournament or a
pickup game at all and that's very depressing. The bottom line is
that when White Wolf does something that hurts the game marginally,
it's felt in some places much more than others.

A public tourney is one at a convention or a game store, where likely
players are congregating.

the visibility of the game.

Jyhad cards, at which point we would tell them their Jyhad cards were

Messages.Body:
"bspaul" <bspa...@excite.com> wrote in message news:1185895872.3...@d55g2000hsg.googlegroups.com...
> Time to address some more points.
>
> First, does it really matter if CCP = WW?

(whatever...no...not sure why anyone would argue about this)

> Second, why is there such fear and name calling when it comes to
> someone who might be playing the game you play for a different reason
> than you? Are you really any better than they are? Why are you
> treating someone like they are ridden with vampiric disease if they
> are playing the game for a reason you don't agree with-at least it's a
> new face/player?

I didn't see a lot of ad hominen attacks (outside of Norm and, er,
"Blinky") but I did see a lot of good, unaddressed points people
made about this. Games tend to only work as good sources of
entertainment when everyone is on more or less the same page
about their purpose. Hell, people get all torqued at one another
over the issue of playing for first-or-nothing vs. playing for the
best placement possible (e.g., playing for second when first appears
somewhat unlikely). Do you really think it's sane to say that
throwing people into the mix who care about the money as opposed to
the fun of the game won't diminish or eliminate the fun for others?
Maybe you can make a reasonable argument for "diminish" as opposed to
"eliminate" but you should be able to readily see why those kinds of
players wouldn't be greeted with open arms. Especially by those of
us who have had experience with this sort of invasion in the past.

> Third, maybe an influx of new players will do the game some good.

That's highly disputable. At least, it's disputable whether their
addition would be seen as good on balance, even if they were able to
bring certain positive things to the game. See above as my basis
for believing there would be a powerful downside.

> Fourth, bribes and collusion vs. play to win. It happens but maybe a
> larger prize will help correct the problem. Think about the other
> potential side of the coin. Perhaps we will see finalists going down
> hill in an effort to win it all. What if the event gave the overall
> winner, after the final round, $25K? Would players really start
> making deals or maybe the might just play the game and try to win by
> ousting their prey? It's hard to answer these questions without any
> actual data to review, right?

Sorry, it doesn't wash. The problems with play to win don't have
anything to do with the lack of a desire to win. People have all the
incentive in the world to win as it is. The problem is pure, simple,
and obvious - and you've been around this newsgroup long enough to
see it with your own eyes if you only cared to look. Look at all the
threads that have run on and on as people try to beat an objective
explanation out of LSJ about, "What do I do if a player does X...?"
Time and again it boils down to, "Use your judgement - that's why
you're a judge." Which basically means there IS no objective way
to make a lot of these decisions. There are a number of guidelines
which certainly help and provide a modicum of standardization. But
ultimately, deciding whether a given player is conforming with PtW
or not and *especially* deciding what to do about it when such a
determination has been made is an art, not a technique. And such
kinds of judgement have no place in any high-stakes contest in my
book.

I'm really very dubious whether high-stakes prizes would reduce the
likelihood of PtW incidents and judgements but it doesn't matter,
anyway. In order to fix the problem, they'd need to be reduced to
zero and I'm absolutely sure they wouldn't acomplish that.

Can you say "law suit"? I knew you could...

Fred

Messages.Author: Rodd...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
Honestly.... VtES is a decent CCG....

I was a Magic player and at one point the game changed for me...
different crowd, a lot BO and uneducated people, and the game got
quite expensive.

VtES can certainly be expensive considering all the cards out there
and the number of copies you can have in a deck leads to a lot of
potential money expenditure. In that regard it hinders some people
from doing well, just like with Magic. SO I can relate to the comments
on supporting cash prizes. However, I can't relate to some of the
attitude. Perhaps instead of cash prizes they could give out more
cards and pay for future events and the cost to get to those events.
Thus keeping those people purely playing for cash away.

Who knows... cash can be good, but you would have to deal with many
potential cheaters and claims to cheating. After all you do have
allies and such in the game. It could get cheesy. I think cash prizes
are a good idea with games that are more of a dual or something like
poker. For me, 9 out of 10 times I play poker with a buy in as it is
much more fun and adds to the game. VtES is a different animal.

Messages.Author: Rodd...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
Also, to add a little bit to my comment....

How many people buy cards on here and how many buy them off the net?
And I will tell you an CCG that requires a constant expenditure of
money to stay competitive will scare away some people. I saw some
comparisons when people noted it is a hobby and just look at a guitar.
Bad example. Once you have the guitar it is yours and you don't have
to constantly spend to play it or get better. Part of the problem with
almost any CCG is the need to spend money for cards you don't have
enough of or that you may need for a deck. If you had the cards you
needed and so did everyone else and you did away with rarities and
such then it would let people pay a lot less to just play the game for
fun and competition. I don't have to spend anything to play basketball
at the public court except maybe a basketball... and once you have an
instrument you have it......... CCG's encourage addiction. And if you
are fine with that then cool... but, not too many people are going to
spend most of their extra money on such a game. And because of the
stagnation of VtES with the small group who play it, it does not
encourage new players... and so many VtES players have recognized a
need for new players that they usually make new players feel like just
a body that was needed rather than a new person in the group. I used
to play VtES, but with all the petty arguing, the players who just
wanted a new body, and then seeing the new players leave as they
didn't feel a part of the group is a large part of why I left.
